utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, could you make sure the witness is brought in? (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. Let me tell you that the Judges are not in such a state of excitement that they've been very imperatively knocking on the courtroom's door, it's just our usher who's not used to knocking the three knocks as sometimes it is done in theatres. All right. Good morning to the Prosecution, good morning to the two Defence counsel, and good morning also to our witness, General Blaskic, who is still a witness in this case for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission. Yesterday we received document 666 and 666A. Then after the hearing we looked at it a bit more carefully, and we saw that there were significant substantive errors in the translation. For example, in the title it says, "Vitezovi, PPN subordination." However, in the Croatian original the word "resubordination" or "attachment" was used . Once again, I hear that now it has been misinterpreted. The English translation in writing uses the word "subordination," and the translation of this Croatian word should be "attach," "attach," "attachment," I think that this is a substantive difference. Let's ask General Blaskic what the difference is. Further on in the text itself, where the word "attachment" is being used, it says -- I'm sorry, the interpreters do not understand counsel. "Reassign" was the word. "Reassign" does not precisely define the notation that is denoted by the Croatian word "pretpotcinjavanje." Since we are talking about key words in the text, I suggest that this document be translated once again and, if necessary, we should clarify the difference between the word "attach", "reassign," and "subordination," and this can be done through further questioning of General Blaskic to see what the military terminological differences are. Although the interpreters who are interpreting here in this courtroom know the terminology very well but probably the text were translated by translators who are not familiar with this terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo, but before asking Mr. Blaskic for some explanations, I'd like to say that Mr. Blaskic has had all the time he needed to give all the explanations he felt were necessary, but I would like to say also that this text was read by your client yesterday and that yesterday he read it in its Serbo-Croatian version, and the answer interpreted it as something that was saying that the Vitezovi were placed under his orders. So it does seem that the Vitezovi were placed under his command. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I remember in this courtroom it was interpreted properly, so that's why I didn't have any objections. However, this piece of paper is evidence. In a month or two we're the not going to remember what the interpretation was in this courtroom but we're going to be reading the document. That's why I wanted this document to be translated in light with what it actually says in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nobilo. I agree basically, but what I want to stress is that yesterday, in answer to a question put to him by Judge Shahabuddeen, the witness said it was always necessary to have an attachment order delivered in order for him to have full authority over the troops. So here the attachment is very officially explained. At any rate, I would like to hear what Mr. Kehoe has to say on this. If necessary, we will ask for a new translation of this text, but for the time being, what I can notice is that the Defence is asking for the Serbo-Croatian word to be translated by the word "attachment." Mr. Kehoe, what you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but there is a substantive difference between "attachment" and "subordination" from the point of view of substance. There is a very significant difference. Colonel Blaskic had different authority when a unit was subordinated to him and different authority when it was attached to him. There is a difference in authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I quite agree that it is a major difference and a substantive difference, but for some time now Mr. Blaskic has been telling us that as far as Ahmici is concerned, the troops had been attached to him on April 16th at 11.52, and because the Vitezovi had only been attached to him at that date and that time, he did not feel responsible for what happened on the 16th of April earlier on in the morning. Could we have Mr. Kehoe's opinion on this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. I, of course, am in the same position as Your Honours in that I do not speak the language. This particular document was translated by the official translation is section of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, not a translation section for the Prosecution or Defence. It's the Court's translation. If there is a discrepancy in the translation, and this is a search for truth that all of us want, I simply ask the registrar to give the document back to the translation section and have them take another look at the document. If there is a change in the document or something is wrong with the document, I think we all want to work a document that is as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't think that's a problem at all. We can give the document back to the translation section. Mr. Nobilo, what do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours need to know what it says and you need to know today while the questioning of the witness is going on. We have expert translators here at the Court's disposal. Let's read the word and they can translate it. If it means "subordination," they will say so. If it means "attachment" in it's technical, precise meaning, then we will hear it from them. We think the Court needs to know while it's hearing the testimony. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges have decided that the document will be read out very slowly by Mr. Nobilo and then the interpreters will immediately give us a precise translation of the text and that will enable us to go forward with the cross-examination. All right. Thank you to all of you. Mr. Nobilo, I will now ask you to read this document, in toto, very slowly and the interpreters will be especially wary of what they're going to say. They are always very wary, so it's hardly useful for me to say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Before it is read, could we please see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The heading says: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and the Croatian Defence Council." Then: "Main staff, registry number 01-93/93. Mostar. 19th January, 1993." On the right-hand side it says: "Defence. Military secret. Strictly confidential." The title of the document is: "PPN, Vitezovi. Attachment." It is addressed to the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. This is what is says on the right-hand side and "To the PPN Vitezovi." After that there is a new title that says: "Order," and the text reads as follows: "The PPN Vitezovi is attached in all matters to Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. I forbid any kind of action on their own. This order remains in force until I personally change it. "Head of the main staff of the HVO HZ-HB, General Milivoj Petkovic. Signed and sealed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kehoe, do you have any questions you would like to put to the witness on that particular change in terminology?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In due course, Mr. President. Not at this juncture. I will conduct the examination on this document in due course and at the period of time when I would like to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well then. So you may continue on the other matters you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Judge Rodrigues has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Nobilo, I think that the word that we find in the document "subordination," in the English document, I don't think it has been translated. If I look at the transcript now, I see that we see "Vitezovi PPN," and then through other -- and then I think that the word that was in question, "subordination," I think this particular word has the not been translated. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may inject since I was listening to the English translation and my colleague heard only -- he didn't hear anything because I was reading the Serbo-Croat. After Mr. Nobilo read "PPN Vitezovi," he read the word appearing underneath it in the Serbo-Croat original and it was translated in the English as "attachment." I don't know what the French translation was, I wasn't listening and I couldn't presume to be able to translate it myself, but it may be "attachment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It has been translated. Yes, it has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, do you have a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, the English translation reaching me used the words "I forbid any kind of action on their own." General Petkovic wrote that in an order. Would that not mean to you, as the commanding officer, that the Vitezovi could not use armed force in any circumstances on their own, that is to say, without your previous approval?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the order on attachment, the direct line of command is being preserved, that is to say, from the main staff or the defence ministry vis-à-vis the Vitezovi, and I acquire the right only to use the unit in combat action and to give them combat assignments without any other kind of command authority; that is to say, I cannot replace anyone, I cannot discipline anyone. However, the Vitezovi, although they were attached to me, they could receive orders from their direct superior commanders, that is to say, the main staff or the Ministry of Defence; that is to say, that their structure was not changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me try to follow you. Then do I understand you to be saying this, that as a result of General Petkovic's order, the Vitezovi could act on your instructions; they could also act on the instructions of the ministry which controlled them. What they could not do is to act entirely on their own. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If one reads this document and acts in accordance with it, they could not act on their own. However, in document 250, the Vitezovi send reports on their activity, which can be seen on page number 4, to their superiors, that is to say, the head of the defence department and the chief of the main staff. That is what it says verbatim, "Report 2-091/93 on the 15th of March", but they did not send reports to me about their activity, and I do not know whether at every point in time the commander of the Vitezovi got assignments for their activity from the defence department or the main staff. If he acted correctly, adhering to this order, then he had to ask for approval, instructions, and orders from the main staff and the defence department. However, the core of the matter is that the direct line of command in the chain of command was not changed by the order on attachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you one further question: Before you were cloaked with authority by General Petkovic's order, the Vitezovi would have been exclusively under the command of the ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The ministry or the main staff, depending on how the minister regulated this -- I don't know the relationship between the ministry and the main staff -- however, at any rate, this is their direct chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: During that period before you came into the picture, was there any situation in which the Vitezovi could act independently, on their own, without the approval of any superior body?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In document 250, they invoke many orders. Sometimes these are orders of the commander of Vitezovi and sometimes these are orders that they received from the chief of the main staff or the Ministry of Defence. However, I do not know whether, in each and every situation, the commander of the Vitezovi reported to his immediate superiors his intentions or not because he did not inform me about that. For example, it would happen that the unit would go to Stolac, and I would find out about it only a few days later after they came back. Whether he had orders or not, I do not have any direct knowledge about that because I was not involved in that chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So what should I conclude? That before you came into the picture, the Vitezovi could or could not act on their own, that is to say, without the approval of some superior body?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I already said that I was not in this chain of command and I do not have any precise information on this. I would find out only subsequently, after this action, that they had acted. But whether they acted independently or not, that I do not know because I did not receive this report from them either. They sent this to their superiors. The incidents they created, whether this was a consequence of independent action or whether it was a consequence of the orders they received, that I do not have any direct knowledge about because they have their own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I ask you that because of the words used by General Petkovic. He said, "I forbid any kind of action on their own," thereby implying, so it seems to me, that they could previously have acted on their own.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that we had problems at the Travnik front lines vis-à-vis the Republika Srpska in terms of some of their reconnaissance which often ended with arbitrary opening of fire and infringing upon the momentary situation. Commanders did complain to me about this. However, the commander of the Vitezovi always pointed out that he was acting on orders from his immediate superiors and I think that around the 5th of January, he sent a report in writing to the command of the Operative Zone that he was independent, autonomous, and that he was entitled to combat action throughout the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and I was not in a position to see whether these kind of actions of his and incidents were on the orders of his superiors or not, but I often had problems because of such activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right, General. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, thank you. Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. General Blaskic, because of Judge Shahabuddeen's questions, I feel I have to put a few questions to you myself. Maybe Judge Rodrigues will have the same feeling. My question is a very short one and maybe your answer will be as concise as my question: Do you think this order is clear, or do you consider it to be somewhat ambiguous? I mean, when you received this order, what was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really cannot recall what I thought at that particular moment when I received it but the order is clear, if we state "attachment," then we know what is implied by the word "pretpotcinjavanje," that is to say, "attachment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. So I see it is clear for you. In such a case, you consider this order to be, globally speaking, very clear. So when it is said that the Vitezovi, in all matters, are attached to you and when it is forbidden for the Vitezovi to take any actions on their own, one must conclude that that includes combat operations.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, had the chief of the main staff meant to subordinate the Vitezovi to me, he would have used the word "subordinate," and then I would be superior and in command for all the activities of the Vitezovi. But with this attachment order, I had only two possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You remember telling us, speaking of Ahmici, that the Vitezovi were attached to you on April 16th at -- oh, sorry, which was the military police. I'm sorry. I had the impression it was the Vitezovi. Maybe it was the --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the military, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. But it seems to me that in terms of hierarchical subordination, it was more or less the same, because the military police, as far as you were concerned, were still subordinated to the Ministry of Defence, and it was on that particular occasion, I remember it well, that you told us a lot about this concept of "attachment."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I said that the direct chain of command was not changed, that is to say, the direct line, chain, and structure remained the same. I was just receiving a unit which was to service me, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, I gather, when we'll talk about Ahmici and the military police. But then my next question will be this: When you received this order, did you feel the need to ask for additional comments from General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really cannot remember the circumstances and my reactions to the order. I don't remember whether I commented on it with General Petkovic or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: My last question: When General Petkovic sends you this order, as it is worded, is he not, in a way, putting you in a situation where you find yourself obliged to exercise a certain control on the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With that order, I did not gain all the competencies in control and command. I could issue combat orders, but I could not, on the basis of that order, discipline a soldier or replace an officer from that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did you transmit this order to the Vitezovi's commander?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not transmit it because he was one of the addressees, and I do believe that he, in fact, received the order himself, a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you can see, can't you, that since General Petkovic is attaching the Vitezovi to you, it would not have been totally absurd for him to issue a two-line order reminding the Vitezovi of the fact that from then on, they are attached to you, and you haven't deemed it necessary for such an order to be issued, have you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my chronology of events, I have noted all my efforts to contact the command of the Vitezovi. I had my requests a day previously, my chronology. I also had a meeting with my commanders on the 21st of January and then asked for the command of the Vitezovi, so my efforts were registered, were noted, when I asked to have a meeting with the command of the Vitezovi, but he was very often inaccessible to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But the wording "I forbid any action on their own" does include combat operations; don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes, that that is what it says and that it includes combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, and if you do not consider that the Vitezovi are subordinated to you and if, at the same time, you consider that the Vitezovi cannot launch a combat operation, I ask myself: Why did General Petkovic send you this order which is basically useless? Why are the Vitezovi attached to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I -- Mr. President, I received a different interpretation twice, may I say? And as I say, I cannot remember all the circumstances, the circumstances under which this document arrived, but I can only suppose that it was the time when combat readiness was being raised, the level of it, and I see that the Vitezovi, directly from General Petkovic, received orders to raise their combat readiness, and they informed him personally of that, and that is contained in document 250 and it is obvious from that document. But he did not subordinate the Vitezovi to me, he attached them to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are not answering my question. My question is the following: When you received this order, did you ask yourself what would be the use of it? If you are logical with yourself, you have to admit that it did not have any use for you; it was not a useful thing for you to have the Vitezovi attached to you, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At all events, Your Honours and Mr. President, it could enable me the right to regulate any excesses made by the Vitezovi, incidents, that is to say, at the Novi Travnik and Travnik front line, and I can only suppose that that was the motive because commanders came to me to complain about the conduct of that unit along that front line against the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is that what you think, or are you sure about this? The events took place six years ago, so my question actually applies to that particular time frame. You were Colonel Blaskic at the time. You receive this order. You see that General Petkovic is attaching the Vitezovi to you. You see that General Petkovic forbids any combat operation and you see that this order applies until General Petkovic emits another order, and yet you do not feel the need to ask General Petkovic for additional comment because you feel quite certain of the way you have to interpret this. So my question remains the same: What is the use of such an order? What was the use of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll try and answer your questions. First of all, I said that I can only assume, that is to say, I'm not certain about this part because a lot of time has elapsed and there were many different situations. I can only suppose or assume, that is to say, I profoundly believe that in view of the circumstances and in view of my notes and the complaints that were coming in with regard to the conduct of those soldiers, that is one thing. As far as combat assignments go, we can see from document 250 that they retained combat orders and their chain of command of the structure of it from the Defence Minister and that they informed him in writing and not myself. Had I assigned combat duties, then they would have reported to me about those combat duties. Next, what use were the Vitezovi to me? Had I -- well, I didn't need them. They just created problems. I asked the joint command to dislocate them to Mostar so that they could serve those people who set them up and formed them in the first place. So I asked myself this question very frequently. I spent one year to change that chain of command and the Vitezovi, at my initiative, became the 3rd Army Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So after all, General Blaskic, this order is not as clear as you first said it was. You yourself wondered about it. You weren't sure of what attachment meant and what was the use of it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said in very precise terms. Perhaps the interpretation was not correct, Mr. President. I said I did not know of what use the Vitezovi were and there was a destruction in the creation, the structure of armed force, but I didn't understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, but if on January 19th you, Colonel Blaskic, you don't know what the use of a combat unit is, and if you don't know what the use of attaching to you a combat unit is, and if you don't feel the need to ask for additional comment, then there is something I don't understand and you must help me on this.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I shall be willing to do so, Mr. President, willing to understand. In my document dated September 1992, I request that that same unit be defined with regard to structure and formation. So as early on as September 1992 I wrote this request. Why? Because it was a unit which had been set up from the HOS units, from the Zenica, Travnik, and Novi Travnik region. It retained its independence, autonomy, and complete independence of me as the commander. Instead of my initiative and request being accepted and adopted and a unit be formed, they just received new insignia and got even more command possibilities then they had when they were the special purpose units. They got even more independence. So my initiatives and my requests were not favourable to somebody, and I think that we can see this because in September 1992, which was very early on, I just asked that their structure and status be precisely defined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're increasing my confusion, General Blaskic. You're worrying me any further, because you're saying that in September 1992 you were already asking yourself some questions about the Vitezovi. In January 1993 you receive an order by which the Vitezovi are attached to you. Let me take an example. Let's take a situation where there is a bad legal officer in the International Tribunal here in The Hague, a legal officer who is not a very able legal expert. He is attached to me in January 1999. At the very same time, I am told by the Registry -- I forbid him to accomplish any legal work. Let's say the legal equivalent of combat operations. A legal expert is meant to do some legal work. The Vitezovi were meant to lead some combat operations. If as early as December 1992 I began to wonder about this legal expert, when this legal expert is attached to me later on and when I hear the Registry say to me, "He is attached to you but he is forbidden to achieve any legal work," I feel I would have gone to see Mrs. De Sampayo and tell her, "Well, what am I suppose today do with this legal expert? What is the use of his being attached is to me? He is supposed to work on legal matters and yet you forbid him to do so and yet you attach him to me at the same time." Your answer when you tell me that in September 1992 you are asking yourself a question on the Vitezovi, it reminds me to put to you this question: Why didn't you ask General Petkovic for some additional information? How can you tell me that this order for you is very clear and not ambiguous at all?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would have been very lucky had my command possibilities been at least equal to the way in which this International Tribunal functions. I did not ask myself the question in September 1992. I raised the question and sent it to my superiors, at that particular date. I took the initiative throughout. The problem was who had created this kind of set-up of the armed forces? Yesterday we saw that the Ministry of Defence issued commands to every policeman at the checkpoints in document -- in the document yesterday and our point 8. So the problem is the structure and who set up that structure, who formed them in the first place. That is where the difficulty lies. My initiatives did, of course, request time, and I wanted to have the unit dismantled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General. Judge Rodrigues now has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General, I have a question to put to you myself. It seems that you established some kind of difference. I'm looking at the English text, so I hope I'm not going to make life more difficult for the interpreters, but do you establish a difference between, "Shall be reassigned in all matters," and, "Shall be reassigned"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My command authorisation was the same if we use the term "attachment." So if the order says "attachment," then I understand that and that is what I acted upon, that is to say, I can use the unit for combat operations and I have the right to issue a combat assignment without a direct change in command, that is to say, I can discipline a soldier, replace a soldier, influence logistics and all the rest of it, which I would have had the term "subordinate" been used, "directly subordinated to," et cetera, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The following question is more or less identical to the first one: Why does General Petkovic say, "Reassigned in all matters"? Why did he specify "in all matters"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I cannot remember the circumstances that governed the situation and what he had in mind, Your Honours, at the time that he wrote the order. I can make a comment, give you my personal comments, but I don't think it may correspond to what General Petkovic had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So I'm entitled to conclude the following: For you, saying "reassigned" and saying "reassigned in all matters" is one in the same thing?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If the order is attachment, then I have the same level of command authorisation, that is to say, I do not gain any greater command authorisation whether it states "in all matters," or not "in all matters." The word "attachment" is the keyword.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another question: Did you, on other occasions, receive other attachment orders?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive other attachment orders. There were situations of that kind, yes, when I received orders about attachment. I received orders about direct subordination as well. There were orders of that kind too. So depending on the situation while I was on active duty, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In these orders, these other orders that you received, what were the words used? Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, for the most part they were terms, and that is the way we communicated, whether they were orders or whatever, but we used two terms or whatever. But we used two terms, the term "attachment," all units are attached to you, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So the most frequent expression was "reassigned"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We're talking about attachment, then, yes, "attachment." I cannot give you an example, such and such a unit will be attached to you for such and such an assignment or for such and such an operation, whereas if we were dealing with subordination, then the order will be that a certain unit would be subordinated to a certain commander, the command of a certain brigade or Operative Zone or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: To conclude, General Blaskic, would it have been possible that General Petkovic specify in that order that the Vitezovi were attached to you for one specific action?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That would have been possible as well, for a concrete action. I haven't got the document to be able to read it in its entirety, but that would have been a possibility, yes. This is done for one operation, one particular operation, or one particular action, or activity. Let us take, for example, that we had to dislocate a unit from one region to another, or that an ambush had to be conducted, or a sabotage operation, or reconnaissance operation, or any kind of activity of this kind. That is what is usually done. If it is an action or operation, then the term "attachment" is used where attachment is completed once the operation is completed. Then that unit would be returned to its previous structure of chain and command, to its previous set-up structure and formation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So one is entitled to say that there was a general attachment for all operations, and that is the reason why General Petkovic said that this order should remain in force until he personally indicates something to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and that is what he stated in his order, that it would remain in force up until the moment that he was to inform me or the commander of Vitezovi that the situation had changed. As a rule, he would have to inform both of us about this, and as he said that he would do so, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You have helped me to better understand this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge Shahabuddeen, I would like the interpreters to take document 657. Do the interpreters have this document with them? It's a Serbo-Croatian document. Maybe, Mr. Nobilo, I can help me before giving the floor to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is in Serbo-Croatian, Your Honour, and French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So it's not an order that a decision -- a decision signed by Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Jadranko Prlic, Mr. President, who is president of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Of course, I will need the help of the interpreters who work from B/C/S into French here. Mr. Nobilo, I also need you to help me. Let's see if we have not made a mistake on another document. I'm doing this, of course, in the interest of the establishment of the truth. I'm talking about Prosecution Exhibit 657. Have you found that Exhibit, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I see what you mean. The translation is a good one here. In point 2, the word "subordination" was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Precisely, but don't anticipate on my question. The remark I want to make is linked to what is said in Serbo-Croatian, so it is with great humility that I am turning to you, Mr. Nobilo, and to the interpreters. I notice that in the translation of point 2 there is a word that has the same root -- I'm sorry, how do you say this? Can the interpreters help me? All right. Does this word have the same root as we find General Petkovic's order?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps I can explain, Mr. President. The word "subordinated" corresponds to the Croatian word "potcinjavanje," whereas the word "attachment," "attach," corresponds to the word "pretpotcinjavanje." So it is made up of two words, "pretpotcinjavanje" and "potcinjavanje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Right. I think it's very interesting, from the witness's point of view. The prefix "pod" has introduced the notion of subordination, whereas the prefix "pre" in Exhibit 657 introduces the concept of attachment. Am I right and can this be confirmed by the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be better to do it this way: The basic word is "potcinjavanje." If to that basic word you add the prefix "pret," then you get a different meaning to the word. You obtain "pretpotcinjavanje."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters add "attachment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So we agree to say that the word "pretpotcinjavanje" means "attachment," and the French translation in Exhibit 657 said that the units were going under the control of had this expression corresponds to this Serbo-Croatian word "pretpotcinjavanje." Right. So I will ask, Mr. Registrar, that the translation section give us a translation of all the terms linked to this notion of attachment, control, subordination, et cetera. Do you understand me, Mr. Registrar? You will officially make a demand to the translation section in the name of the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have finished my Serbo-Croatian class. Thank you to the interpreters. Judge Shahabuddeen, I believe you had another question to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General Blaskic, it is half a question on a very short document. I don't believe I shall be raising any of the problems of translation to which this document gave rise. I want to ask you a different question. The document was signed by General Petkovic, describing himself as chief of HVO, Croatian Defence Council, GS main staff. Could you tell us what kind of authority did General Petkovic have to issue this document? More particularly, did you understand him to be saying that the Vitezovi was already an integral part of the HVO and within the command structure of the HVO of which he was chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that this structure was changed quite a few times and it was rather dynamic, this structure and this establishment. However, I believe that General Petkovic had authority from the Minister of Defence, and possibly from the commander in chief, to command those units or to command them at a given point in time. But I know that the members of those units signed contracts with the Ministry of Defence, and from the point of view of logistics, they were directly supplied by the Ministry of Defence, and they also received the salary for their work from the Ministry of Defence. And in which period of time General Petkovic commanded these units and in which periods the Ministry of Defence commanded these units, that I do not know precisely, but from document 250, I can see -- which surprises me a bit -- that General Petkovic issues an order on the 14th of October that the units should go to the front line, and the Ministry of Defence issues an order saying that the units should return from the front line later. It would be more logical that the person who orders the unit to go to the front line orders its return from the front line. So there were probably authorities that were interwoven at this point because the structure was changing and this was the process of the creation of this army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm sure you will have the opportunity to go back on this document, which is particularly interesting. I will now ask you to continue either on this document or on something else. It's all up to you, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, in light of Your Honours' questions, I would like to ask a few follow-up questions based on some of the matters that Your Honours just highlighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that you are quite free to lead your cross-examination as you deem it necessary, but I do think it would be more logical for you to go on by going back on the questions put to the witness by myself and my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you were asked a question by Judge Rodrigues concerning the reason for the attachment of the Vitezovi. Now, you recall that we talked yesterday that the order on Bosnian soldiers subordinating themselves to the HVO was to be complied with by 1900 hours on the 20th of January, 1993, and I reference you to the order that was just highlighted by Judge Jorda, Exhibit 658. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had the decision of the Prime Minister, Dr. Jadranko Prlic, in my hands a few minutes ago. Could I just have a look at this or could I have it in my hands so that I could see what the term is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly, General. Exhibit 658, if I could, Mr. Registrar? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was speaking of 657, Mr. Kehoe, not 658.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was my error, Mr. President. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On 658, in paragraph 3, General, it calls for the resubordination and the sanctions for any refusal for resubordination, i.e., the units will "be regarded as paramilitary units and shall be disarmed and arrested." And the deadline for the carrying out of this order is listed in item 7 of Mr. Stojic's order, and that deadline is 1900 hours on 20 January, 1993. Now, General, with that knowledge in mind, do you believe that Milivoj Petkovic, Brigadier Petkovic, knew of this order from his superior, Bruno Stojic, when he issued Exhibit 666, the subordination order of the Vitezovi, to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: "Attachment," Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. "Attachment," Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Attachment order 666.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not a quick study, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you understand my question, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take your time, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. I didn't hear it. I was reading document 658, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question to you is: Do you think that when Milivoj Petkovic attached the Vitezovi to you on the 19th of January, he knew of Bruno Stojic's order that units should "be disarmed and arrested" that didn't place themselves under your command by 1900 on the 20th of January? Do you think that Petkovic knew of Stojic's order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This order, document 658, it is certain that Milivoj Petkovic and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina knew about this and the Minister of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and even more so because in point 8 of this document, Bruno Stojic says, and I quote: "For the implementation of this order, it is the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO Armed Forces and of the Administration of the HVO Military Police that will be responsible to me for carrying out this order." But, Your Honours, as for disarming, according to document 658, I did not issue such an order to my subordinates, and please bear in mind document 405 or 404, this is a Defence Exhibit, and that is the order issued by Milivoj Petkovic, that is to say, 01-111/93 of the 20th of January, 1993, where it says: "With a view to reducing tensions, I order," and then point 1: "1. Establish contact with the competent command of the authority of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the zone of your responsibility --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a second, General Blaskic. For the debate to go on in an orderly manner, I want to check something. This was a preliminary question, Mr. Kehoe, wasn't it? I think the question was to know whether or not, in your opinion, Mr. Milivoj Petkovic was aware of the order issued by Bruno Stojic. Was that it, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So, please, give some time to Mr. Kehoe to put his questions to you in full before making any comment. You can go on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, given that fact, for what operation was the Vitezovi attached to you on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I do not recall any specific action except for the things that the Vitezovi did at the front line against the army of Republika Srpska. I cannot really remember what kind of operation was in question, but I can confirm that as for disarming the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we did not plan any kind of action of that nature in the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, prior to this time, all through 1992, the Vitezovi was deployed to the front line in Jajce, for instance, on numerous occasions, and you didn't need this additional order on the 19th to deploy the Vitezovi to the front line there, did you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have not seen the document, but as far as I can remember, I did not send the Vitezovi to Jajce. They were in Stolac when they were needed the most in Jajce. They did this on orders that they received from their superiors. As far as I can remember now, I did not issue any orders to them saying that they should go to the front line in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, how long did this attachment last, the attachment that General Petkovic notes, "This order shall remain in force until I personally change it"? How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly how long this lasted because it's been a long time since then, but I know that this system was changed for sure and the Vitezovi retained their independence, which can be seen from document 250 and the report that they sent to their direct superior --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question was simply how long it lasted, and you noted that you can't recall. Now, we have numerous facts in your chronology, General. Is it anywhere listed in your chronology how long this particular attachment lasted?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I cannot recall, that I would have to look through my chronology to see whether I noted it down somewhere when the Vitezovi regained their independence but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, on the break, why don't you do that for us? Why don't you take your chronology and peruse through it and see in there -- give us the notation as to when the Vitezovi or this particular order ceased. Now, General, my next question concerns a comment that you made concerning this attachment, and again, correct me if I'm wrong, I believe it was in regard to a question asked by Judge Rodrigues, and you noted that you received this attachment because you received complaints that were coming in about the Vitezovi soldiers, and my question to you, General, is: What were these complaints?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I remember well. On one occasion, a weapon was missing from the zone of responsibility of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade at the front line, and the commander suspected that groups from that unit simply came to the front line and took this weapon away with them, and the situation was similar in Travnik Brigade, in sector number 1. Also, there was a recoilless gun, this was an anti-armour gun, it was missing too, and they thought that the Vitezovi had taken that too. The commander from the Travnik Brigade had reported this to me. And also at the front line, they were infringing upon discipline all over, and this was something I knew, that they would not tell the commander of the sector that they were carrying out reconnaissance activity and that they were carrying out independent actions at that particular front line; that is to say, for the most part, there were such activities at the Travnik and Novi Travnik front lines. There were also other incidents. Specifically, I cannot recall all of them now because I did not go into all the details. I tried to resolve this problem through the system itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the system solved the problem by Milivoj Petkovic attaching the Vitezovi to you until further notice to all parties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that this was one of the attempts made but this did not resolve the problem. They kept the direct chain of command, and this is reflected by document 250. If you read this document more carefully, you will see that in that period, the Vitezovi did not send their reports to me. They were sending reports to Milivoj Petkovic and Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let us clarify an issue on Exhibit 250 and let us talk about the remarks on Exhibit 250, and if you could look at that document, I have a couple of questions for you because you've been talking about this report at some length. Turn to the "Remarks" section of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we should put this on the ELMO because the Judges don't have this document before them right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us read this first paragraph on the "Remarks" section. Do you see that, Mr. Usher? I believe it is the second to -- third-to-last page in the English version, you see "Remark" at the bottom. That's it. "Remark: "The army base Dubravica - Krizancevo Selo was situated at the first line of defence. During a strong attack by MOS --" That's "Muslim defence forces." " -- a fire broke out in the storeroom and part of the archive. That is the reason why some of my reports or sections of reports are not backed up by documents. There is worse: when I came back from Herzegovina, the computer was missing, and most of the archives had been on its disk." If we turn to the next page, Mr. Usher, about midway down, you will see the words "All this." That's it right there, right in the centre. "All this is just the essential summary, because it would be impossible to write the whole history of 'Vitezovi' in a few pages." So by the author's own admission, General, this particular report, as the Vitezovi was being phased out of existence, does not encompass all of the records and everything that happened to the Vitezovi during their existence, does it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not claim that the report was a complete one, I do not have any insight into the Vitezovi reports, but I did say that they informed the chief of the main staff and the Minister of Defence about their activities, and it says here on the 15th of March, 1993, and there is the number of the report and all the other details are there. Also at the time when this report was written, the head of the Vitezovi was also the deputy head of SIS, and I think that he had high command responsibilities and he had access to computers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let us continue to talk about these complaints that you are receiving concerning the Vitezovi prior to this attachment order on the 19th. Did you receive orders that Vitezovi soldiers had committed war crimes, prior to this attachment?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, as far as I can recall -- you're asking me about a period of time which is six or already seven years ago -- I cannot recall having received such complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you did receive complaints concerning crimes that they had committed against Muslims, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what period you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, turn to your chronology. I mean, you read the information out concerning problems with the Vitezovi in early January, so let's go back to your chronology and let's talk about what you read to the Court.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that's the way you should tell me, the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, the reference point is the order of January 19th. Now, prior to January 19th, had you received information about the Vitezovi committing crimes against the Muslims? And while you're looking -- I don't want to limit you in any fashion to your gathering of such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Maybe this is a good time to take a break because it would enable the witness to go through his chronology, but I also want to remind all of you that the break is also meant for everyone to take a break, a rest. I was thinking of a 20-minute break, but maybe we can have a rather longer break for the witness to be able, at the same time, to look through his chronology and to take a rest. That's important. So, Mr. Kehoe, I think the best thing maybe is for you to go on for a few minutes on that particular issue -- no, wait. Let's take a break and resume our work a little before noon. That will enable the witness to look through his notes and to take a rest. Yes, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would like the witness to look for two issues. The first issue has to do with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, be specific about what you want him to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first issue pertains to my questions regarding the length of this attachment and how long Petkovic attached the Vitezovi to Blaskic. It's a question I asked probably 15 minutes ago. My second question is his information concerning crimes committed by the Vitezovi prior to the 19th of January that he recited during his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Is it clear for the Defence? Is it clear for the witness? Yes. Very well. We will resume a little before noon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. You may all be seated. Mr. Kehoe, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, during the break did you have a chance to review your chronology?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't hear what you said. I wasn't getting the interpretation. It's okay now though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the break did you have a chance to review your chronology?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I wasn't able to look through all my chronology. I did look through a part of it, but as there is so many of it I didn't get a chance to go through it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's see if we can answer this question based on what you did go through. When you went through your chronology, did your chronology demonstrate when the Vitezovi or the attachment of the Vitezovi to you by Milivoj Petkovic ended?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I haven't got that noted in my chronology, just that I do not know when the two documents actually started. But I do know that when I returned again to the Vitez military district on the 4th of March 1993, that the circumstances were the same as they were before the 19th of January. The Vitezovi were acting, that is to say, as an independent unit. I believe that was the period that -- the relevant period. From the 19th of January to February 1993, particularly as in Exhibit 250 I read that the command of the Vitezovi referred to the chief of the main staff and the Defence Minister and sent him a report on his activities in the January conflict and was not referring to me as the command of the Operative Zone. However, I was not able to find in my chronology a note on when the beginning was and when it ended. Perhaps this is because I was isolated in Kiseljak for the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, in looking at Exhibit 250, when the Vitezovi went to Busovaca to engage in combat activities, it would appear, would it not, that they were attached to you at that point?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, quite possibly they were. Probably they were attached, but they -- I did not issue orders to the Vitezovi to go to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted, during the course of a meeting with Mr. Flemming and Mr. Merdan that took place on the 5th of February, 1993, and for record purposes, counsel, it's page 18267, you note as follows, during this meeting on the 5th of February, 1993, and this is your testimony: A After that Merdan said that the civilians were being taken to do trench digging. Q Where? What place? A Busovaca, and that was the time that I was confronted with the statement of this kind because we had numerous meetings, Dzemo and I, before that I and the commander of the 3rd Corps. And he also ascertained that the Vitezovi were dealing with problems in the individual villages by using ultimatums, and he had in mind Bosnian Muslim villages. Now, this is a meeting that you testified about on the 5th of February, 1993, and my question, General, is when the Vitezovi was dealing with these Bosnian Muslim villages through ultimatums, were they attached to you pursuant to Milivoj Petkovic's order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that I'm not sure when that order was pulled back by Milivoj Petkovic. Perhaps they were attached, but activities of that kind they did not undertake by my order. They never received an order by me, as Dzemo Merdan said, to settle problems by means of ultimatum in the Bosniak villages. Let me just look at my chronology for a moment. I asked Mr. Merdan to tell me where and how they were solving problems by ultimatum, but at that meeting Merdan did not continue to explain and said nothing. So I asked that Mr. Merdan be more concrete and specific, and to tell us where the Vitezovi were settling problems by means of ultimatums. I understood him to mean the Vitez municipality, that that was where they were doing it. But what villages, because the municipality of Vitez had many villages, and what kind of ultimatums? He didn't answer that question. He didn't say anything to my question, but I just received this information. As far as trench digging was concerned, that is true. It was the first time, and Mr. Dzemo Merdan repeated several times this assertion. However, throughout the time in Kiseljak, which is where I was, no Bosniak Muslim was -- who was detained dug trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. General --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You asked me about digging trenches, as far as I understood. You mentioned the question at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During this period of time, you got information from Merdan that the Vitezovi were presenting ultimatums to Bosnian Muslim villages. What did you do with that information, General? What did you personally do with that information?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A complete report from the meeting, as indeed from every other meeting, I sent on to the chief of the main staff, including what was stated by Dzemo Merdan, Mr. Flemming, and myself at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have that report, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not have any of the reports, apart from the ones that you have succeeded in gathering yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you confront Darko Kraljevic on this issue?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, for two months I was not in a situation in which I could go to the command headquarters. I was not able to be there, but before that, I had undertaken certain steps. I think it was the 18th of January. There's a document. Whether it was 204, 206, or 208, which indicates the measures I undertook to prevent non-soldier-like behaviour, criminal behaviour, and violent behaviour, and that document illustrates my efforts to prevent this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let's be as accurate as possible. You received this information from General Merdan on the 5th of February, 1993, and you returned back to your headquarters in the Hotel Vitez on the 3rd of March, 1993, less than one month later. My question for you, General, when you got back to your headquarters after the 3rd of March, at any point did you call Kraljevic in and demand an explanation as to what he and his soldiers were doing concerning these ultimatums?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those ultimatums, up until the 5th, no longer reflected themselves in Dzemo Merdan's behaviour, nor were they repeated from that meeting of the 5th of February. There were many other meetings with Dzemo Merdan. He never expressed viewpoints of this kind with regard to the behaviour of the Vitezovi any more, but already on the 4th of March, I organised a meeting with my associates, and I would have to have a look to see whether Mr. Kraljevic came to the meeting or not. May I take a look in my chronology, please? In my chronology, I don't have it that Mr. Kraljevic was at the meeting. Probably the situation reverted to its autonomy, what I was talking about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, the fact is that you never even asked Darko Kraljevic about these ultimatums presented to these Bosnian Muslim villages at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that the order on attachment does not give me the right to undertake disciplinary measures. Second, I was not in a position at that time, while I was in Kiseljak, to discuss this matter with him. I would also like to add that I informed the chief of the main staff about that in my regular reports that I sent off from each of my meetings. From every meeting held, my chief of staff would get a report from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, prior to the attachment on the 19th, what crimes had the Vitezovi committed that you were aware of? This is prior to the 19th of January, 1993, when Petkovic issued this order of attachment, Exhibit 666.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, that there was violence in January and that the units brought in from Herzegovina had taken part and that the Vitezovi had participated. I undertook measures for the security service to inform me about each of these incidents and to inform their superiors too. I think that 204 and 206 exhibits reflect that, reflect everything that was done to stop activities of this kind on the part of the Vitezovis. It was a crime to steal weapons as well from the Travnik battlefront, but there was violence in the towns as well on both sides, both by the special purpose units and the members of the HVO, as well as the BH army units. However, that violence was conducted for profit more or less. It was profiteering more or less rather than nationalistic goals. The target was the rich people, both Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you knew, prior to the 19th of January, that the Vitezovi had criminal elements in their midst; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That there were individuals who had perpetrated acts of this kind. According to the reports from the security service I knew about this, and I took measures and issued orders and demanded that the competent authorities be informed thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let me ask you about your comment to the Judges about your request to remove the Vitezovi from Central Bosnia, again with regard to documentation to support that claim. Do you have any documentation among all the records that you have to support your claim that you requested that the Vitezovi be removed from Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my chronology, I have this noted down. It was at a meeting of the joint command. Next, I have records of a talk, I think it was a talk with Mr. Prkacin as the head in the joint command, and that talk was introduced into my wartime diary. I haven't got the wartime diary here with me, but I do have a note on it in my chronology, that a request of that kind had been sent out. If necessary, I can look at the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you do not have any documentation to show the Court to support your claim that you asked for the removal of the Vitezovi; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just like to object to this type of cross-examination. The accused is not here to prove that it is his fault that he has not found a document. If the Prosecution wants to make an assertion, it is up to the Prosecution to prove it. I think that it has been legally posed in the wrong way, saying "Why haven't you got any documentation?" on an event. It is up to the Prosecutor to prove matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nobilo, I think it is maybe also the accused's role, who is right now a witness -- let us not make a mistake -- right now General Blaskic is a witness, and as such, he has a number of duties. He has the rights of a witness but also the duties of a witness, and he also has the rights of an accused. I would like to remind us all that when one of the parties, be it the Defence or the Prosecution, puts a question to General Blaskic, who is now a witness, the witness has to justify what he is saying. A moment ago, the witness said, "I took a number of measures." Fine. We understand that. He took a number of measures. But the Judges may deem it necessary to ask him what kind of measures he took. I understand the nature of your objection, but I think you have to nuance it. Of course, generally speaking, the Prosecutor has the burden of proof and he must prove that the accused has committed such and such a crime, but right now the accused is a witness, and when the witness says something, of course, he is entitled not to bring forward any kind of document, and in that situation, the Judges will take note of the fact that he has not brought a document forward, but in that case, I think the Prosecution was just saying, "Well, then, you don't have a document." So I understand your objection, but I think you have to qualify it somewhat in view of the situation the witness General Blaskic finds himself in. Yes, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I agree with you, that the Prosecutor can ask and the witness answer, not have the document, but he is asking it in an accusatory manner. Now, it is not our fault that the Croatian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina does not cooperate with the Defence. It is not the Defence's fault for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that the parties have to help the Judges in all manners possible. The Judges have the responsibility of establishing the truth. The Prosecutor put a question to the witness and then, later on, he said, "So you don't have a document." Of course, the witness answers as he wishes. He can say, "I didn't have the time to find it." A moment ago, let me remind you the Chamber said, "Of course, the witness needs to have some time to look through his chronology and to find this document." Don't forget, Mr. Nobilo, that you will have the possibility to ask the witness further questions and you will have the possibility to give him a chance to bring forward other documents. We will move on. General Blaskic, you may have had time during this slight exchange of views to find some information, some documents maybe? As an accused, you also have the right to say, "I don't have this document here with me right now. I don't want to have us lose more time than is necessary. I'm sure I have this document somewhere or I have this evidence somewhere." You can also say that.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was not able to look through my entire chronology, but I found an event on the 15th of November, '92, when the commander of the Vitezovi took into custody Mr. Dzemo Merdan. Mr. Prkacin was with me then, a member of the joint command, and I requested the commander of the Vitezovi to free General Merdan, and after that I discussed the matter with Prkacin and asked him to do what he could to have the Vitezovi withdrawn to Mostar. But I have other requests of that kind. I would just have to go through my chronology of events to find other examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might just have one moment, Mr. President? I just want to ask a question to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move on, General, and, again, I am following up on some of your statements that you gave to the Judges this morning, and the one I would like to direct your attention to, General, has to do with the difference you drew between direct subordination orders and attachments. My first question for you on this, General, is: When did you receive direct subordination orders? And within that answer, please tell us for which units you received such direct subordination orders.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just one moment so I can look up the date, please. On the 23rd of July, 1993, the unit was the military police at the time when I found myself in the encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that the only subordination order that you received?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? I wasn't receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the time when you were the commander of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, was this order the only subordination order that you received?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I don't think it was the only one, but I cannot at this point in time remember the exact date of another. I also received an order linked to the dismantling of all the units and the formation of the 3rd Guards Brigade. I think that that was sometime in January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, my question with regard to that subordination order, was that subordination order in existence until you left as commander of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which one? There were two. The first or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Maybe I misunderstood you, General. You said there are two subordination orders. Let's talk about both of them in sequence.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the Washington Agreement was signed and after the encirclement stopped, the military police returned to its old formation and system where the head of the military police directly commanded the military police, and the 3rd Guards Brigade, after it was formed, remained when I left, it remained subordinate to the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and the units were completely extinguished, such as the Vitezovi, the Light Assault Brigade and the other ones that went up to form the 3rd Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, other than the military police, General, did you receive any subordination orders for other units, such as Tvrtko or Zuti or any other units?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I also received them for the Tvrtko unit, but it was not on a rank with these units, that its reorganisation and dismantling be started. I would have to look at my chronology to see when. The Tvrtko was a special purposes unit of the B type compared to the Vitezovi which were the A type.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What about Zuti? Did you receive a subordination order with regard to the Zuti special purposes unit?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Possibly this was at the same time, but I'm not sure. I would have to look this up in the chronology, when Tvrtko took place and whether they were of the same rank or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, tell me, General, what was the need? I mean, why were these units subordinated to you as opposed to attached to you? What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Always, I always asked -- I mean, in all my efforts -- that all units be subordinated to the commander, and from September 1992, in my documents, I showed this unnatural establishment because the situation was such, objectively speaking, that there were several chains of command, and the formal responsibility went along one line, or perhaps to put it better, I was in a position to be responsible for the actions of those units over which I did not have any command or any other powers in the zone of responsibility of Central Bosnia. At the time of attachment too, they were in a position to receive orders from their immediate superiors to carry out such orders and not inform me about this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is: With regard to these individual units and why some units were subordinated and why some were attached, your answer is that the attachment order was made so they could take orders from other entities? Is that your answer? And if it's not, please clarify. Feel free to clarify it, please.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I asked that their structure be defined, and those were my requests. Obviously, they only went up to that instance, that is to say, limited responsibility. The superiors, those who were superior to me, only attached units to me. Why the levels that were superior to me retained such a structure and why they created it at all, that is to say, that they could issue orders without informing me? Well, it's hard for me to answer that. But I expressed my views orally, and in writing, and at meetings when I had the opportunity to do so. I said that this was a mistake in the actual set-up and through those bylaws, the act on the armed forces is being infringed upon, where it says that the command is one, then in practice there is not one. Why did they only attach rather than completely subordinate units? Perhaps there were other reasons that my superiors had for doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let us go back to where we left off yesterday and, again, we are talking about events both in Gornji Vakuf and in Central Bosnia, Vitez, Busovaca, on approximately the 19th of January, the date when you got this attachment order from General Petkovic. Now, you met Brigadier Cordy-Simpson, did you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, many times in '92 and '93. I don't know what meeting you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Generally did you consider General Cordy-Simpson a competent and reasonable person?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that he was a reasonable person, yes. That's what I thought. But for me to judge how competent an officer he is -- I saw him at meetings, I heard what he had to say at meetings, and this is a high officer, an officer of high standing, but I did not have any direct knowledge about him. I didn't know where he served before. I don't know his biography. I have very little information about him. I don't even know which armed service he belonged to, but I can talk about any one of these meetings because I have them noted down in my chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let me read you Brigadier Cordy-Simpson's assessment of the situation in Central Bosnia as of the 19th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm referring, Mr. President and Your Honours, to Exhibit 406/43. The cover page is of the 20th of January, but the actual report is for the 19th of January, 1993. I'm talking about the top of the second page. If we could put that page -- I'm sorry. I do believe that this has got to be in closed session. I take that back. I believe it has to be in private session. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe this is a document that we would have to read in private session, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We shall go into private session then. Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 668.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, Prosecutor's Exhibit 668 is a British Battalion military information summary from 20 January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I would first like to read the insert for Gornji Vakuf at the bottom of the page that starts with "D. Assessment" and following up to the next page. Do you see that at the bottom of the page you're looking at? It says, "D. Assessment." Keep going down that page, Mr. Usher. Right down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this is the assessment for Gornji Vakuf of the British Battalion: "Assessment. B company assess that the original HVO plan for Gornji Vakuf was to secure the outer villages, cordon the town, bisect it, and then clear each area in turn.
