The HVO initially assessed that this could be achieved fairly rapidly. The main axis of HVO advance onto the town appear to have been Pidris, Mracaj, Uricje to the junction at grid reference," and they give a particular grid reference. "It is thought that the Bosnian BiH/Muslim resolve has been greatly underestimated. In addition, a great deal of HVO artillery fire has proved ineffective, falling mainly on Muslim residential areas and not close to the main concentration of Muslim fighters. In short, HVO have met with only partial success and have not managed to break into the town itself. B company express concern that similar problems could possibly erupt in Jablanica and, therefore, affect another MSR into Central Bosnia. The possibility of similar eruptions in Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez is assessed as considerable." If we could move to the bottom of that page, Mr. Usher, on the insert that reads, "Four. Busovaca." "The BiH in Busovaca have erected a new checkpoint at Kacuni ..." With the grid reference. "This is the only BiH checkpoint en route from Vitez to Kiseljak and is located just north of the BiH Brigade HQ. The checkpoint itself is well manned by approx. 15 - 20 soldiers who are equipped with automatic weapons and an RPG7. Reports from 1 Cheshire (call signs) during daylight hours stated that the BiH had laid a number of mines at the checkpoint. Subsequent information from the Dutch transport squadron suggested that the mines may have been lifted as darkness fell. Comment: This is yet another indication of the spread of mistrust throughout the Busovaca/Travnik/Vitez area. Comment ends." Now, General, clearly on the 20th of January, 1993, or prior to that time, hostilities are taking place in Gornji Vakuf. Would you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Slow down a bit, Mr. Kehoe. The interpreters have some difficulty following you. They just ended the translation of the text you have been reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, clearly on the 20th of January of 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please wait, Mr. Kehoe. Give them a little time to end what you have been saying a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. It's okay now, Mr. Kehoe. You can put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, clearly on the 20th of January and prior to the 20th of January, hostilities were taking place in Gornji Vakuf between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and would you agree with me, General, that the setting up of the checkpoint in Kacuni, on the 20th of January by the Muslims, was a reaction to that conflict?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, how can I agree if you are claiming that the checkpoint in Kacuni is a reaction to the conflict in Gornji Vakuf? Look at the map. We've marked the roads up to Vitez. I can mark that road too. Geographically, this is a divided area. There are mountains that divide it. There was never an asphalt road between Gornji Vakuf and Novi Travnik. Never, ever. What happened in Gornji Vakuf could have caused concern and, judging by what you described, this is not a checkpoint, this is a military barricade. We are talking about 15 or 20 soldiers. We're talking about RPGs. So we are talking about hand-held armour-piercing weapons, we're talking about mines placed on the road. We are not saying whether they are anti-tank or anti-personnel mines. And a checkpoint is a checkpoint where there are two policemen with a notebook, a pen, and small arms, and they are noting the vehicles that pass by, et cetera. And during my testimony, I said -- well, I didn't have the opportunity of saying this because the questions were not put that way. There were checkpoints all over, and this was the last one in a series. There was a checkpoint in Kruscica and at Pavlovica on the 18th of January, on the 14th of -- first, in Sebecic, et cetera, and the checkpoint in Kacuni was put up by the 1st and 7th Travnik Brigade, which was then later called the 1st and 7th Krajina Brigades. But that was a barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were the HVO checkpoints in Busovaca, both the town and the municipality, on the 20th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a reaction, as a reaction to such a checkpoint, perhaps it was established, but I don't know. I moved along the road. I did not see a checkpoint on the road from Kiseljak to Vitez, I never saw one that was stronger from the point of view of the military and weapons and soldiers than the one in Kacuni that was held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the civilian police had checkpoints and they regulated the traffic. This was at the Kaonik crossroads. This is the main intersection, the road going to Busovaca and the one going to Kakanj, Visoko, Vares, et cetera. Mostly there were civilian police checkpoints. And then during the night between the 20th and the 21st of January, whether a checkpoint was put up, I don't know, especially not by way of a barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, keeping in mind the deadline for the disarmament of 1900 hours on the 20th of January, 1993, did you order additional troops, HVO troops, to travel from Kiseljak and Kresevo to the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Until the 20th? The only --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will clarify my question. On or before the 20th of January, did you order additional troops, HVO troops, to travel from Kresevo and Kiseljak to Busovaca, keeping in mind, General, that the deadline for the disarmament was 1900 hours on the 20th of January?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those troops from Kresevo and Kiseljak, every week, that is to say, every week, before the 20th of January, they would go to sector 1 in Travnik to the front line facing the Serbs, but these were regular shifts, and I would tour them together with the commanders of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and, on the 20th of January, troops from Kiseljak and Kresevo did arrive at the front line. They took over this duty, as recorded, at the front line against the Serbs, and I did order, though, that troops from Busovaca, from the village of Katici, had to go to the front line, although they expressed their concern to me. They said that they were concerned over the fact that the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were piling up near their villages, and I told my co-workers there is no need to avoid their responsibilities at the front line vis-à-vis the Serbs, so the soldiers should go and do their shift and they did go. But this was not a special order I issued on the 20th. This was longstanding practice I think from November 1992. I have this in my chronology and I can exactly say which document this is and which date this is when we organised a defence in the area of Travnik in this way, and not only from Kiseljak but also Kresevo, from Fojnica, and, for a certain period of time, from Vares and Kakanj and Zenica too. All municipalities took part in the defence of the municipality of Travnik or, rather, the municipalities of Central Bosnia, and also from Vitez and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to go to another document. I don't whether you want to break for lunch or have me continue on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you can put this last document to the witness and then we'll take the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's look at another document, General.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 669.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this is another military information summary from the British Battalion. And, Mr. Usher, I'm interested in page 2, section 2, the report on Busovaca. Do you see that? THE USHER: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the date of that document? January 21st? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The 21st, Mr. President. And I will attempt, Mr. President, Your Honours, and for the sake of the booth, to read this as slowly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Two. Busovaca. "Reference our milinfosum 81 dated 20 Jan. '93, paragraph 4. Dutch transport squadron report that the new BiH checkpoint placed in Kacuni at --" With the grid reference. "-- was put in place to prevent HVO reinforcements coming from the Kiseljak/Kresevo. The local BiH commander states that these reinforcements arrived during the evening of 20 Jan. '93 and were turned back at the checkpoint. Tensions increased in Busovaca during late afternoon. Between 2000 hours - 2100 hours 2 x HVO checkpoints were erected at either end of the town centre ..." And it gives the two grid references. "At approx. the same time a quad 4 X .50 mounted on a flat bed was deployed on the road south of the town in the area of ..." And it gives a grid reference. "All main routes in and out of Busovaca were then controlled. Between 2100 hours 20 Jan. and 0200 hours 21 Jan. '93 the Dutch transport squadron reported a number of explosions in the town. On 21 Jan. '93 a daylight recce confirmed that 8 shops/kiosks had been badly damaged by fire and some form of explosive. Dutch transport believe that these shops which are all Muslim were possibly damaged by grenades. Both HVO checkpoints were removed on 21 Jan. '93. A local source reported to the Dutch battalion that a number of families in Busovaca had sent their children to stay with friends in Zenica. Comment: The action of 20/21 Jan. '93 appears to be a pre-planned, co-ordinated attack on the Muslim population. Comment ends." Now, I have additional questions with regard to this issue, Mr. President, that I'm sure we can address after lunch. They were somewhat extensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well then. We will adjourn and resume our work at 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Mr. Kehoe, I would just like to remind that before the lunch break you gave the witness a document, and you've waited until after the break to put your question to the witness about that document, which we will not reread once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, but before that particular series of questions, if I can take a document out of turn which I neglected to put in when we were talking about the Novi Travnik incident back in October of 1992. I would like to do that at this time, and it is a letter from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's your choice, Mr. Kehoe. You're quite free to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It is a letter from President Izetbegovic to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 670, 670A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have some extra copies for the booths. I think it would be helpful for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can the booth go and meet the usher, please, so that we don't lose too much time? Thank you. In these cases, Mr. Registrar, if you could lend a hand, because the usher goes one way, maybe you could go the other way.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Jorda, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is my fault. I should have done this ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can see that for once the Prosecution has made a mistake. Mr. Kehoe, we're listening to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a letter from President Izetbegovic to president Franjo Tudjman dated 27 October, 1992. "Mr. President, recent events in Bosnia and Herzegovina have compelled me to address you with this letter. "HVO units have systematically provoked conflicts in Novi Travnik, Vitez, and Prozor, in which there were casualties and destruction. All the roads through Western Herzegovina have been closed even for humanitarian aid. At the same time, a propaganda war against Bosnia and Herzegovina and its legal authorities is being waged in the Croatian media. They have invented and are continually repeating news of an alleged coup d'etat in Bosnia-Herzegovina, speculating about the changes in the government and persistently ignoring the struggle by the BH army against the Chetniks being waged under extremely unequal conditions. The idea is to morally finish off our people, who have suffered hard physical blows from the Chetniks, and leave us without any hope. It seems that the Croatian media have accepted this second part of the job. "As you know, the truth is that there has been no coup d'etat in Sarajevo. "The truth is that the BH army is fighting bravely in Gorazde, Sarajevo, Konjic, Jajce, Gradacac, Zepce, Maglaj, Visegrad, Brcko, and other places, and the whole world knows that with the exception of the Croatian TV. Why are they ignoring this and spreading despair? "The truth is also that tanks fired at and entered the town of Prozor but these were not the tanks of the BH army. "Our military equipment, which is of decisive importance in resisting the Chetnik invasion, has been stopped in Zagreb and Grude. The consequences are evident. "Negotiations about the future system of Bosnia-Herzegovina are going on in Zenica while at the same time a policy of fait accompli is being implemented by force thus degrading the negotiations in Geneva and making them pointless. "The HVO has crossed the line of legitimate defence against the Chetniks and embarked on the systematic destruction of legal civilian authorities and the establishment of quasi-state institutions. "Overall, there is a clear impression that they want to use the difficult situation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, maybe the most difficult one in its history, to impose a solution which is contrary to the will of most of its citizens. "Which reasonable people in domestic and international public could believe that while waging hard battles against the Chetniks, we have simultaneously opened a front against the HVO? Does this not remind you of that Chetnik story that we are bombing ourselves in Sarajevo? "Bosnia and Herzegovina will never accept division on exclusively ethnic grounds or any solution imposed by force. It has enough forces for its own resistance and enough friends in the world. "Bosnia and Herzegovina considered Croatia and its people especially as being among these friends. In spite of all, we will continue to believe in this friendship and act accordingly. "We ask you kindly, Mr. President, to use your unquestionable influence to remove the obstacles along this road so that our relations can develop in accordance with the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation between our countries. "Please receive the assurances of my highest consideration. "President of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic." It is addressed to Dr. Franjo Tudjman, President of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to move back, at this juncture, back to our Exhibit 669, which is the military information summary of the British Battalion of the 21st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Kehoe. This letter, had it been published in the media at the time or was it a confidential letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, Mr. President. I can find out, and I can ask the authorities in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina whether it was a public letter or not. I simply don't know and I don't want to say anything one way or the other, but I will find out. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges will ask you, Mr. Kehoe, to try to know whether or not at the time it was written or later on this letter was publicized or maybe public anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will make that inquiry as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let me turn our attention to the report of the attack in Busovaca on the evening of the 20th of January, 1993. Now, we spoke about the deadline for the disarmament being 1900 on the 20th of January, 1993, and this particular situation report reflects the erection of checkpoints at either end of the town centre in Busovaca one hour later at 2100 on the 20th of January 1993. Did you order the erection of those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The checkpoints in Busovaca, I did not order their erection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know about them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 20th of January I did not know of them, because I had probably gone through Busovaca earlier. I knew about the checkpoint in Kacuni, but let me make my comment to that. It is exact that the order was up until 1900 but with regard to the order that we're discussing, I convened a meeting of all the subordinate commanders, and at that meeting I said that not a single unit of the HVO would disarm the units of the BH army and that we would wait for an agreement as to how this was to be done between General Petkovic and General Halilovic, their agreement. From document 405, Defence Exhibit 405, it is visible that General Petkovic sent us the assignment of setting up contact with the BH army and settle the question on the basis of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, there was a flatbed truck placed in the town centre, according to the BritBat military information summary. Did you order the presence of that flatbed truck, with the anti-aircraft weapon mounted on it, in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not order that flatbed truck to come to the centre of town. I see from these reports information about that, reports sent in by the members of UNPROFOR, but I was aware of the fact that a checkpoint did exist at Kacuni. I know that it is not true that it was the role of that checkpoint to prevent any kind of reinforcements from Kiseljak, because the shifts at the Travnik front line --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, that's not the question. The question was with regard to the flatbed truck.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The flatbed truck. I did not order it to be there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who ordered the erection of the checkpoints and the presence of the flatbed truck with the anti-aircraft weapon in Busovaca town centre?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know who ordered it. I was not informed of that. But I do know that I myself, at a meeting on the 21st of January, 1993, requested --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I must interrupt you again. That's not the answer to the question. You said you didn't know who did it and we'll move on from there. After the attack that took place in Busovaca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I can see you wanting to make an objection, but I don't agree with your silent objection. I think the witness has to answer the questions put to him. The question was a very clear one. He doesn't know, he doesn't know. That's very clear and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He said he didn't know and then he said "But I do know" and then he was cut off. Is that fair, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, because I think the Prosecutor got the answer to the question he had put to the witness, Mr. Hayman. That's all. When you ask a question, you wait for an answer. The answer was given. Let's move forward to another question; otherwise, we'll lose a lot of time. And from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I know that we should avoid losing any time. I don't know if it's Rule 89 or 90(G) that says so. But, Mr. Prosecutor, put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But every witness in this trial has been allowed some opportunity to explain their answers, and we would ask the accused be treated the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Of course. But, Mr. Hayman, I don't think that your client, who is the witness right now -- and let me remind you of that because sometimes it seems there is a bit of confusion on that -- he is a witness, he is under oath, and he has to answer the questions put to him, and the Judges are here to make sure that the questions put to him are precise enough, and I think in this case, it is precise. Who gave that order? Does the witness know? In which case, it's fine, he doesn't know, and he says so, and then we move on to another question. But I can see that I myself, I am making the Prosecutor lose some time. So, Mr. Prosecutor, put your new question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let us look at the tape that is taken by the Dutch transport battalion that we provided to the booth, and it is Prosecutor's Exhibit 238. If I can just note for the record, Mr. President, with regard to this tape, this particular tape was submitted in a closed session with a closed-session witness. However, the tape itself need not be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then it can be read and examined in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can move to that tape, Prosecutor's 238? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, the evening of the 20th and the 21st of January, businesses belonging to Bosnian Muslims were destroyed throughout or in the town of Bosnia (sic) during that night-time period, weren't they? Excuse me, I'm talking about the town of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that there were individual crimes committed in the course of that day or, rather, that evening, and I heard witnesses testifying here, I think it was a Defence witness, Slavko Katava, who spoke about this and said that the civilian police conducted an investigation and wrote reports with regard to individual criminal acts, terrorist acts, with the individual perpetrators in the town of Busovaca, he brought many documents with him, and I believe that in the official notes and records that he has, there are indeed some which refer to this destruction of property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read you a portion of a testimony, and if I can just go to private session briefly, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Very short and quickly, please. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session) (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm moving to the next exhibit, and the registrar has a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 671.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this Exhibit 671 is another British Battalion information summary from 3rd of January, 1993, and the section, Mr. Usher, that I'm interested in discussing is part 3 at the bottom of page 1, going over to the top of page 2, and it reads as follows: "An LO team --" Meaning "Liaison Officer" team. "-- spoke with Edin Beganovic at the BiH HQ of the 333rd Brigade at Kacuni. Edin stated that he was the officer responsible for morale, information and religion. He believed that the Muslims in Busovaca (between the ages 15-65) had been arrested and detained either at the secondary school at Busovaca or the Mediapan factory ..." And it gives a grid reference. "Edin reported that the conflict had started when the Muslims had ignored the HVO demands to hand in their weapons on the 20th Jan. Approximately fifty HVO extremists led by Anto Sliskovic were then reported to have destroyed many Muslim properties and to have killed one BiH soldier on the night 20/21 Jan. Edin reported that 50-100 BiH soldiers who lived in the northern part of Busovaca started to prepare defensive positions on Kardic hill ..." With a grid reference. "The HVO persuaded the BiH soldiers to give up their defensive positions and these soldiers were subsequently arrested." Now, this military information summary, General, reflects that there was, in fact, a demand by the HVO to the BiH to disarm; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that the HVO, that is to say, I myself, as the commander, and commanders subordinate to me, never received an order of that kind, that is, to start the disarmament of the BH army. At a meeting with Dzemo Merdan, and during the conflict in Novi Travnik, he said that somebody -- the pretext was that somebody had asked the Territorial Defence to hand in their arms, and I claim that the HVO never issued a request of that kind and I also claim that this man, Mr. Divanovic, did not expound the role of the barricade at Kacuni and bringing in the 17th Krajina Brigade in Kacuni and bringing into Lasva, Dusina, and Vjesnica soldiers from the 3rd Corps, from Zenica, and the attachment of the forces of the 1st Corps of the operative group of Visoko to the forces of the 3rd Corps and their engagement against the HVO in the area of Busovaca and the Kiseljak municipality, although that is the front line against the Serbs. Also, the convoy intended for Srbrenica, it was not mentioned that it was a forerunner to the conflict. When you asked me a moment ago who started, it is difficult for me to assess who started with the incident because I was in Kiseljak at the time and the incident occurred in Kacuni, up at the barricade there, and I know for a fact that further action evolved, and I am convinced that it was according to the 3rd Corps plan and the result was the corridor between Bilalovac and Kacuni. Whether there were individual actions, we saw on the tape a moment ago that there were individual terrorist acts, and that comes under the authority of the civil police. If a name was found and if it was ascertained that the soldiers had done it, then it would have been up to the military district court and military authorities but, at all events, we dealt with the question of the disturbance of law and order, of course within the frameworks of our competencies and within the frameworks of the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, this particular attack on the Bosnian Muslims commenced one hour after the expiration of the Bruno Stojic deadline. Do you think that was a coincidence, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know which attack you're talking about. I'm not aware of any attack, but I know that on the 22nd of January, the commander of the 333rd Brigade from Busovaca, that is to say, of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, met with the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in order to negotiate about resolving all incidents by way of dialogue and peaceful means, that is to say, that there were incidents with the barricade and other things from both sides, and they met in order to resolve this problem through dialogue. That is the kind of order that my commanders received from me, and this is document 405 that I keep invoking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will talk about 405, General. This particular document, this milinfosum reads that: "Approximately 50 HVO extremists, led by Anto Sliskovic, were then reported to have destroyed many Muslim properties." Anto Sliskovic was a man who worked for you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is a man, if we're referring to the same Anto Sliskovic, who was my assistant for security. He worked for the administration for security from Mostar. That is a man who was directly subordinated to the security administration in Mostar. He was my assistant for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this is the same Anto Sliskovic that you sent to Busovaca to gain information about the release of Sead Sinanbasic in August of 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is the same man who, through his own line of work, was in touch with the persons in authority in the civilian police. He intervened so that Mr. Sead Sinanbasic would be released from the custody of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the same man that you assigned the investigation regarding the crimes in Ahmici to, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because he was in charge as security assistant. He was the only one who was in charge of carrying out an investigation overall, including myself, my command, and all other forces that were in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did you ever order an investigation of the participation of the HVO military in these attacks on Bosnian Muslim property in Busovaca on the evening of the 20th of January? Did you ever order such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that this kind of investigation was carried out by the civilian police, and I asked that I be informed about this event and all events. I was informed about this at the meeting with all commanders, where the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade submitted a report on everything that happened in Busovaca, because it wasn't only that that was going on, there were also wounded soldiers of the HVO. They were wounded by the troops of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the zone of responsibility of these brigades. Also, a lot of Bosniak Muslims were moving out even earlier on, from Busovaca towards Zenica and Fojnica, and he submitted a report on that situation. However, an investigation on individual terrorist criminal acts were carried out by the civilian police in cooperation with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. In this investigation by the civilian police and the military police, was anybody ever charged and, if so, who and what punishment did they receive?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All the reports would have to be looked into, all that were brought in by Slavko Katava and, also, his official notes to see what they handed over to the military district court to is see how this was taken care of by the district military court. I did not have the powers to exercise any kind of control over the district military court because this court was under the jurisdiction of justice and administration and under the Ministry of Defence. I said that I received information on all crimes, that is, the total number of crimes committed over the first three months. I spoke about that yesterday or the day before yesterday. These were 92 crimes, and 31 criminal reports were filed to the district military court, out of which certain rulings were passed, but there are five or seven levels between that and the individual perpetrator. I was not in charge of carrying out investigations of this sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, you were in charge of ensuring that HVO soldiers in your brigades, who were criminals, no longer continued to remain in your brigades, isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you see, you're talking about soldiers in my brigade. I was not commander of that brigade. I was commander of the Operative Zone, of a corps. In order to understand what we are talking about, I was certainly creating the system, and I was passing orders as of September 1992 onwards. I also invoked one of the documents, I think, on the 18th of January, 1993, that the protagonists of crimes should be dealt with and the protagonists of crime should be sent away from HVO units. But I wanted to have a system created, one that would operate. I personally could not chase each and every individual perpetrator. Where would I have gone to if I dealt with each and every individual?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you telling this Court that you were not -- as the overall commander, you were not responsible for ensuring that brigades under your commands didn't have criminals in their midst? Are you saying that wasn't your responsibility and it was only the responsibility of the brigades?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no. That's not the way I put it. Maybe I have been misunderstood, but when you're asking me about discipline, allow me to explain. If a soldier commits a disciplinary mistake --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, I would like you to try to give a very precise answer to the question put to you by the Prosecutor. Please try to concentrate and try to help us. You say you set up a system and at the same time you tell us that no, you were not the commander of the brigade, that you were the superior commander. So that superior commander, does he have authority over the brigade commanders? Please concentrate on the particular question that has just been put to you by the Prosecutor. He just asked you if you thought you were not responsible for the operations of the brigade, who were under your orders apparently. So did you have any authority over the brigades that were under your command in terms of criminal acts that they might have perpetrated?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had authority over the brigades, and I had responsibility, military responsibility, for the situation in those brigades. However, the Prosecutor is saying don't I think that I was in charge? Yes, I was in charge, but I was creating a system, a system of repression that would lead to the building of military discipline. That is to say, a system that would make it possible for a platoon commander to take military action against a soldier of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you did have authority over them. You set up a system that was meant to be even more efficient but, still, you were in charge in terms of the chain of command. You had authority over the brigades and over the acts that were perpetrated by the members of these brigades. We agree on that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I am aware of the system, Mr. President, if a soldier commits a crime, then the military police carries out an investigation in terms of that soldier, and then a criminal report is filed with the district military prosecutor, and it is the prosecutor who is in charge further on. That is to say, if he decides to initiate proceedings, then all of this belongs to the jurisdiction of the district military court. However, if the prosecutor returned the criminal report to me or the commander of the brigade, then it is the commander of the brigade who is in charge or I, personally, if this was returned to me within the scope of our own responsibility. We are supposed to take military disciplinary action. I'm sorry for being too fast. It is the district military court that is in charge of crimes, criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. So you were not in charge. I'm just trying to understand. Fine. Mr. Kehoe, put your question again. No. Judge Rodrigues, you would like to put a question to the witness? You, like me, want to understand who was in charge of what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General, I would like to know if at least in the circumstances which prevailed at the time, you could draw up a report or communicate with the military police?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if I got the right interpretation, but I was just asked whether I could draw up a report or in some other way communicate with the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, I was not asking whether you were capable of doing that, I was asking if you had the obligation as a citizen maybe even to do that sort of thing. Supposing you are aware of the fact that someone has committed a crime. Maybe you have direct knowledge of that or maybe you know that because the commander of the brigade has told you about that particular crime. All right. So you know that somebody has committed a crime. In that specific case, did you feel that you were under the obligation, either as commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, either as a simple citizen to communicate to the military police about what has happened? Were you in charge of that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not only as a commander, but as an ordinary citizen. If a crime was committed and if I know of the name and surname of the perpetrator, it is my obligation to submit a criminal report to the district military prosecutor as a citizen or, rather, to notify the crime investigation service of the military police about this, because if a crime is being committed and if I happen to be there, if this happens to be in my immediate vicinity, then I'm supposed to even take care of the crime scene and to leave the traces there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So, General, one is allowed to infer from this that if you were under the obligation to communicate some information to the brigade as a citizen, you were even more so under the obligation to communicate information to the brigade as a commander.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly. If the investigation resulted in a name and surname. As you asked, Your Honour, I have the name and the surname of a perpetrator of a crime. Of course it is my duty to submit a criminal report against this perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I think that Mr. Kehoe can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I'm a bit surprised by this concept that seems to be yours on legal proceedings, because if indeed you have to wait to know the name of the person who has committed a crime before launching any legal procedure against him, then it seems that, you know, it might take some time before you can initiate such proceedings. When you hear about criminal acts happening, you start by saying that a crime has been committed, whereas in your system it seems you have to wait to be able to communicate, the name, surname, address, job, et cetera to the legal authorities before doing anything. It doesn't seem that it should work that day, should it? I mean, as far as legal matters are concerned.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not a lawyer, but if I understood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but we are legal experts.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We specialise in crime, criminal law.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know, and I listened to what the Honourable Judge asked me, and the Honourable Judge said if a crime was committed and if the perpetrator was identified. That's the way I understood it. That is to say, what are my obligations if the perpetrator of a crime is known, identified. That is the way I understood this question. If I find out that a crime was committed and if I don't know who committed it, then, of course, it would be my duty to inform the authorities of the civilian police. As far as I know, in the case of perpetrators unknown, this falls within the scope of work of the civilian police. They are there to protect the law and order. If it happened in military barracks, of course I wouldn't call the civilian police. I'd notify the military police officer on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Even when there is a military police in times of war, General Blaskic? Even when there is a conflict going on, as it was the case, do you go to local police station? Please answer me precisely.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are talking about a town, a town where civilians live. It is the civilian police that has jurisdiction over this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, General Blaskic, we know that there were civilians living in Busovaca. We are talking of a war time situation. You have the military police. I'm not going over that problem of subordination of the military police. I'm simply asking you whether or not you think that in such a situation the military police was only in charge of dealing with the soldiers who are not present at 9.00 for going to bed, or if you think that the military police, in such a situation, is also in charge of leading some investigations on criminal acts committed in the streets of Busovaca. It is your right to tell me that the military police was not in charge of such matters.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The military police certainly cooperates with the civilian police, Mr. President, but this is not a war in Busovaca. In Busovaca, there is still peace. There are only conscripts in Busovaca. They are soldiers only when they are at the Travnik front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. So peace is reigning in Busovaca. We'll stay on that particular thing and, Mr. Kehoe, you may put your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, how many Muslims were killed that night in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have any figures of this nature, that is to say, how many Muslims were killed. I don't know what night you're referring to. What night are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The night of the 20th of January.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have any such figures how many Muslim Bosniaks were killed. I specifically do not have that report. It is probably the commander of the Busovaca Brigade who has that report or the representative of the civilian or military police from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many Bosnian Muslim houses were burnt on that night of the 20th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have such figures as to how many were burned, and I know that there were explosive devices that were thrown at certain facilities and I know that the police did investigate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many Bosnian Muslims, to your knowledge, fled the town of Busovaca after, immediately after, the events on the evening of 20 January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Muslim Bosniaks were running away or, rather, leaving Busovaca, according to the information that I received at the meeting on the 21st of January from the commander of the brigade. He did not tell me the number, but they were leaving Busovaca, and also forces were being brought into the outskirts of Busovaca by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did you bother to take any steps to inquire whether soldiers under your command had been involved in the killings, any burnings, or any of the expulsions of Bosnian Muslims in Busovaca as a result of the events on the night of the 20th? Did you bother to do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. On the 21st of January, 1993, I had a meeting with the commanders where the commander of the Busovaca Brigade was too, and he reported to me on all these events, on all these events in Busovaca over the previous week, including the departures of Bosniak Muslims from Busovaca, but I do not have the names and surnames and other details, but I did have a meeting with him and he did report this to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of one HVO soldier that was either disciplined, removed from the ranks of the HVO military, or criminally charged for his participation in these events on the 20th of January? Can you give us the name of one soldier?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that I took part in the building of the disciplinary system. I did not look into individual names. It is at the level of company, et cetera, in any army that this is done; and even at the level of brigade, it is only numbers that are registered rather than names of individuals. So I told you the numbers. I said that I was aware of 92 crimes. I received information about that. I also have the number of criminal reports, and I know that the military district court looked into this, but as far as the names and surnames are concerned, perhaps I do have it jotted down somewhere in the chronology, but I can't see it here because it was not my practice to write that down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, it would be accurate to say that on the 21st of January, 1993, that the Bosnian Muslim population -- excuse me. Let me re-ask the question. My colleague had a question with regard to my statement. Well, would it be accurate to say, General, that as of the 21st of January, 1993, the Bosnian Muslim population was petrified by the acts inflicted upon them by members of the HVO; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As for these events, there were incidents and there were tensions in Busovaca, Vitez, and Novi Travnik, and they were two-sided. Now we are looking at one side only here; that is to say, in Katici, when I received some information that caused concern, and in Novi Travnik and in Vitez, there were similar incidents, that same day or one of those days, five soldiers from Busovaca were wounded when they were patrolling it. They were wounded by the BH army soldiers, that is to say, that there were tensions there, and most of the tension was in Novi Travnik and Vitez. In Novi Travnik, most of all. And the British troops from UNPROFOR helped us to keep the situation under control there so that it would not escalate into a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So is the answer to my question "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that there was a lot of fear and a lot of concern because of all these events on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the exhibit that you have been talking about, Exhibit 405, Defence Exhibit 405. Now, General, this is your order of 21 January, 1993, at 1355 hours, where, based on an order from the main staff of the 20th of January, you order that the units: "1. Establish contact with the competent command of the BH Army in your zone of responsibility and settle all controversial issues by means of agreement." Now, General, my question to you is, preliminarily, did it strike you that what was taking place in Busovaca on the 20th of January was ethnic cleansing directed towards the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that these were individual acts of terror and that there was violence in Busovaca, that there was violence in Vitez, that there was violence in Novi Travnik, and that I did everything within my power to stop this and not to have this kind of trouble again. I asked the commanders to do everything they could, including the elimination of soldiers who behaved destructively from the HVO units. I think that this order was dated January 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, are you familiar with the phenomena where an army, while the army is ethnically cleansing the area, also negotiates to stop hostilities, and these two events are taking place at the same time? Are you familiar with that phenomena?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind, where ethnic cleansing is occurring and where negotiations are taking place. I only know that I did everything in my power at that particular time to prevent any kind of problems and to solve everything by means of agreement because the balance of forces was in favour of the BH army and it was not in my interests at any point to have a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me re-ask my question, if you didn't understand it, General: Are you familiar with the phenomena where an army is ethnically cleansing an area while also, at the same time, pushing for a cessation of the hostilities through negotiation? Are you familiar with that type of phenomena?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not study it specially, perhaps it exists, but unfortunately I have not had an opportunity to read up on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's look at another document, General.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 672, 672A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look at this document, General. We are not going to read the entire document. Mr. Usher, I would like you to put the second page onto the ELMO. General, is this your document --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can the witness be allowed to read the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He's looking at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He's still reading. Why doesn't counsel ask him, "Have you finished reading the document?" That would be the most courteous and appropriate thing to ask. I know I haven't had a chance to read it in English yet; I am still getting there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have two remarks. First of all, is it really necessary for the witness to read all this document, which is a long document and which has been signed by him? I don't know if it is really necessary. I think it would be better for the Prosecutor to tell us which paragraph he's particularly interested in. Then he could put his question to the witness, and that's the best way to move forward. Then -- this is for the technicians -- if we are in open session, the documents are meant to be shown to the public and therefore should be placed on the ELMO. How many times do I have to say this? I know it's a bit complicated from a technical point of view, I'm not asking of you that it should be done immediately, but I want it to be done each time we're in open session and a document is presented to the witness. Now, Mr. Kehoe, for that question ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, if we just move that down a little bit? The pertinent paragraph is the first full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a document dated the 11th of August, 1992, and is a report on the situation in Central Bosnia, zone of responsibility, between 4 and 10 August, 1992. General, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The document bears the stamp of the command, but it's a little strange that I didn't sign it, and nobody signed it on my behalf either, and it was typed out on a typewriter, so that appears to me to be somewhat strange. May I just look through it a little longer, please? The document isn't signed. It has a stamp but no signature, and I'm wondering why it has no signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Maybe the best would be for us to take a break. This will allow the witness to read the document. And then after we resume our work, Mr. Kehoe, you can put your questions to the witness. I think that's the best way to go about it. Maybe then somebody can also tell us why the signature does not appear on this document, the commander's signature. All right. We'll take a 20-minute break. Oh, sorry, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I note this document is technical in nature. It is talking about axes of movement and it is very technical. Thank you. I think a break, so that the witness can read it, would be great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, and while we're here, I'll just direct the Court's attention to the pertinent paragraph which reads as follows at the top: "The disposition --" And this is talking about the Serbs. "The disposition of enemy forces has remained the same."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Kehoe. We have just said -- just a second. All right, Mr. Kehoe. Quickly, please, because I have just said that we would go over this document after the break, but maybe you want to make another objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear as to what we're talking about here, Mr. President. The paragraph notes that: "The disposition of enemy forces has remained the same. The enemy has been carrying out ethnic cleansing on a daily basis while pushing for a cessation of hostilities with the HVO in negotiations, which would result in the legalisation of the occupied positions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, do you still want your client to read all the document in view of what Mr. Kehoe has just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we are having a break, I think that's a good use of the time. He could still have a moment to rest and read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. A 20-minute break then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Mr. Kehoe, I think that the witness will have had the time to go over this document, so I think you can put your question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The document is from the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, yes. I recognise the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, you were aware of the phenomena of an enemy or an army carrying out ethnic cleansing while pushing for a cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You asked me a question linked to -- quite possibly I understood it incorrectly, but I refer to the report and I recognise this part of the text related to ethnic cleansing which the Serbs perpetrated, as can be seen from this document and from all the events that took place, and in this document too you can see that I focus my attention on events up at the front line against the army of the Republika Srpska but the units of the HVO under my command did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, you're not answering. The question was quite precise and it was a question on a point of principle, if I have understood Mr. Kehoe well. I think he wanted to know whether or not you were aware of that phenomenon, a phenomenon that implies carrying out ethnic cleansing while, at the same time, trying to negotiate something. So he wanted to know whether or not you were aware of that. That's it. Mr. Kehoe, do you have another question you want to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do not, Mr. President. I want to move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Let's see that other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While counsel is finding his next document, we would ask that if the Prosecutor has the chronology referred to in paragraph 3, that it be produced under Rule 68 as exculpatory material. This is apparently a chronology of the TO attacks in the Kiseljak municipality on or about the 8th of August. Those were the attacks at Duhri and the roadblocks at Gomionica which were designed to take control and cut the Kiseljak municipality. If they don't have it, fine. If they have it, we make a Rule 68 demand for it. We've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel and the Court have everything that we have with this document. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'm sorry, I haven't understood Mr. Hayman -- oh, all right. Well, you've just had Mr. Kehoe's answer, Mr. Hayman. All right. The objection is granted, yes. Rule 68 is always in force as long as the trial is under way, so it does mean that the Prosecution has a certain number of obligations to honour. But that's closed. So, Mr. Kehoe, you can submit your other document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next document, Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 673.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this is another entry in the diary of Colonel Stewart from Friday, 22 January, 1993, and I will read the first two paragraphs: "General Morillon visited us today; for the first time - apart from when he came with General Namvbia right at the start of our tour. He arrived slightly late and then we briefed him in the Information Room. After that we went to Gornji Vakuf where all hell continues. The cease-fire lasted until about 0700 hours and then the HVO began attacking the town from the South. It seems the HVO are determined on their course of action and heavy artillery is being used from the South. "Ambassador Beasseau was still there - having spent the night in Gornji Vakuf with Alun Jones. Morillon wanted to meet both sides. Present for talks were Selmo Cikotic, COS to Merdan, and Pia Agiuc - both representing the BiH Army as well Colonel Siljeg and the local HVO Commander Zdenko. The talks were fairly fruitless. Siljeg made impossible demands. We offered to be in the middle between the forces and to man a roadblock. Siljeg said he had to consult and then we broke up. A round came through the Medical Centre windows. It was spent. I travelled back with General Morillon in his staff car. En route we noticed that many of the houses in the village of Bistrica were ablaze. We presumed it was ... ethnic cleansing." I'm sorry. The sentence reads: "We presumed it was HVO ethnic cleansing." Now, General, do you know whether this village around Gornji Vakuf, Bistrica, is a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the area very well because at that time it didn't come under my jurisdiction. But as far as the name says, I can say that I think that it is at least a Croatian-Muslim village, if not a majority Croat village. I am saying this on the basis of my very moderate knowledge. The word "Bistrica" would lead me to conclude that it was a Croatian village because an associate of mine was born in Bistrica, he was in Gornji Vakuf for a short period of time and worked with me, but we could, of course, check that on the population list, census, in Gornji Vakuf. Up until now, I did not know -- I always believed it was, in fact, a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, during this time, you and your headquarters continued to stay in contact with what was happening in Gornji Vakuf; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had general information, daily information, as to the events in Gornji Vakuf, and I received this information from my superiors but I don't know having heard before this meeting the event described by Colonel Stewart. He was at the meeting; I did not have occasion to be. But the events in Gornji Vakuf and in Central Bosnia indicate that there were situations where orders from the main staff did come but were applied differently in Gornji Vakuf to what they were in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me give you another document, General. If I can, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have a question for Mr. Kehoe. This document consists of an original version and a two-page translation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will submit just the top two sheets. This is just an internal document so they can find it in the computer system. So if we can just submit these two pages, Mr. Registrar, and we'll take the other documents back. I'd appreciate that. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 674, 674A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a very brief document, and it is a notice from the duty operative of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone to the Northwest Herzegovina Operative Zone, to the attention of Zeljko Siljeg and the command of the HVO Anti Starcevic Brigade in Gornji Vakuf. The date is 22 January, 1993 at 1645. "We hereby inform you that on 1630 hours we intercepted a message that the Balija are preparing to launch an operation in the area of Pajic Polje." Signed duty operative of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. General, this message came from your headquarters, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Quite possibly it did, but why is there no registration number on the document? It should have had one, a document of this kind. I can't see who signed it, the officer on duty or duty operative. There's no signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, the particular term that is used in here, "Balija," that is a pejorative term used in reference to Muslims; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is a pejorative term for Muslims, and I have already said that 100 witnesses have passed through here and none of them ever maintain that I used that kind of expression ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, would you agree with me that it would appear that members of your staff in your headquarters used that pejorative term in an official document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps some of them did. I say that I cannot see the registration number. Perhaps he used it. Had I noticed it being used, I would have reprimanded him. It was my rule that the allies or the other side were called by their proper names, but quite possibly there were reactions of this kind as well. As I say, I don't know who the officer on duty was, whether it was an individual who had already been expelled and persecuted or had some personal problems and thus this was reflected in their work in this kind of way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this document also reflects, does it not, that the HVO in Central Bosnia had the capability to intercept information that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was passing; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had devices for intercepting radio communication, very modest devices, I might say, and this information shows that they were forces of the 3rd Corps, that is to say, our immediate neighbours, and I can't really say now. It states here that a message was intercepted. Probably it was an open text sent via radio link package. Other forms of interception did not exist, just this radio type of interception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on this document being listed as "Urgent, Urgent," you would agree that this information was extremely important information to be conveyed to the brigade in Gornji Vakuf and the headquarters in Tomislavgrad; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if there is ongoing fighting between two warring parties in an area then every message has its level of importance. This message talks about preparing to launch an operation and it has its importance, whether to allow the negotiating side to know of this, if the negotiating stage had been launched, or to counteract the operation to be launched. So every message has its importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, the bottom line with this document and the other situation reports that we saw from Gornji Vakuf, these documents reflect that there was a degree of coordination between Gornji Vakuf and the Central Bosnia Operative Zone; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're talking about coordination. Coordination in the military terminology has very precisely defined meaning, in the sense of control and command. That is one of functions of control and command. The sense of information and informing existed, so we could not turn a blind eye to what was happening in the immediate vicinity and in which all the forces of the 3rd Corps of the BH army were taking part, but coordination of combat activities or operations did not exist in the sense of control and command. Information about events, of course, existed, mutual informing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, as this battle is ongoing in Gornji Vakuf, back in Busovaca, when did the HVO begin to arrest civilians and in incarcerate them in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which civilians and who within the HVO, a unit, a brigade, a battalion, a company? Tell me the unit you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, within these days, the 20th, 21st, 22nd, 23rd, before you went to Kiseljak, were HVO troops arresting Bosnian Muslim civilians and incarcerating them in these newly built gaols in Kaonik camp, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's like this -- I apologise to the interpreters as well, but I received a double interpretation. First of all, I heard "Muslim forces." I know that you didn't mean Muslim forces arresting Muslims, of course, but were there individual cases, who was arrested, when? Give me the time frame so that I can look back in my chronology. I do not have any facts on the fact that any military formation or squad arrested anybody or carried out arrests. So if arrests were taking place, tell me which units you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, with all due apologies, I was not there and you were the commander, and my question was: When did you get information that HVO soldiers had begun to arrest Bosnian Muslim civilians and incarcerate them in the Kaonik camp? When did you get that information and when did such arrests begin?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Information that military units had done this, I received information on the 27th of January at a meeting with the commander of the 3rd Corps, that is to say, that there were those who had been arrested on both sides. The meeting was chaired by Mr. Cordy-Simpson. The meeting took place in Kiseljak. That is to say that there were soldiers who had been arrested on both sides. It was only later on that I learned that there were civilians among them too. I ordered, on the 27th of January, that all those who had been detained should be released according to the protocol of the International Red Cross, but military formations that had -- whether they had received such orders, they had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us stay with that point. You say you issued an order on the 27th of January that the civilians be released. Were they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That civilians should be released according to the protocol of the International Red Cross. They were not released even on the 5th of February because it was the position, clearly stated by the representatives of the Red Cross, I think that I have it in my chronology, the name of that particular lady, that not all conditions had been created. The basic conditions for prisoners to be released was that there should be a cessation in the fighting and that there should be a stabilisation in the security situation for all the prisoners to be able to be released on both sides, the release of prisoners on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, can I ask you to be more precise in the way you put your question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those prisoners that were held in custody until the end of the first week in February of 1993 were forced to dig trenches on the front lines, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As regards the situation in Kiseljak, I am claiming that not a single one had been digging trenches. I know that my commanders received instructions to the effect that prisoners of war could not be engaged in trench digging. The first time I received information of this or, rather, claims to that effect, Mrs. Iris asked me, on the 5th of February that I investigate her claims. I carried out an investigation, and I received information that no one had ordered this or approved of this, to have prisoners of war taken to dig trenches. My position was this could only be done by soldiers. That is the principle of the former JNA on which I was trained, and that is that a soldier digs his own trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, after you received the information that nobody had ordered these prisoners and civilian prisoners to dig trenches, did you investigate whether, in fact, it was true that HVO soldiers were taking these civilians from the Kaonik camp and taking them to dig trenches? Did you investigate that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I promised that to Mrs. Iris too, and I said that I was isolated in Kiseljak, that I would carry out an investigation but that personally I was not in a position to go because I was isolated, blocked in Kiseljak. I carried out this investigation on the basis of her information on the 5th of February, and I informed her about my findings. Then I also ordered the chief of staff that this should be forbidden, although it was never approved either that the engagement of prisoners of war should be prohibited, that is to say, in terms of trench digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, as with the situation in Busovaca on the 20th of January, let us now talk about what you did when you received information about Bosnian Muslim civilians being forced to dig trenches. Did you discipline any HVO soldiers for forcing Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches? Those Bosnian Muslims that I'm talking about were those released at the end of the first week of February, 1993. Did you discipline anyone and, if you did, give us a name.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Now you are saying when I found out about it. This was in February, but allow me to have a look at the date, please. I had a meeting about this on the 12th of February, 1993. Then a lady who was a Red Cross official informed me about the tragedy that had happened, and I asked for a complete investigation to be carried out on this the matter and, also, this case when two Bosniak Muslims were killed, and this was also taken to the district military court in Vitez. I checked on this on several occasions, that is to say, when the criminal report was first filed and then the investigation carried out by the military police, all the way up to the prosecution itself. I repeat, I specifically had forbidden this. Throughout my stay in Kiseljak, not a single Muslim Bosniak, not a single one, went to dig trenches for anybody's needs, or any other civilian. Soldiers were digging all the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us stay, General, with the incident that you just talked about, on the individuals who were killed while they were digging trenches. Were the individuals who were responsible for that in the HVO, were they charged with a crime, did they go to gaol, and were they removed from the HVO military ranks?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have information that they were removed at that point when the investigation was started and also when the indictment was there against those persons and when also this was prosecuted by the district military court in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I presume this is public information. Do you have any documentation in your possession to support what you just said?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right now, I do not have such information here with me. I already said that I was not in charge of personally supervising the work of the district military court, but I did receive information on several occasions that the procedure against these persons is an ongoing thing, that is to say, against the perpetrators, the persons responsible for that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many others were disciplined, to your knowledge, for forcing Bosnian Muslim civilians to dig trenches? And the Bosnian Muslim civilians that I'm talking about are those that were incarcerated in the Kaonik camp up until the end of February 1993. How many?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that I had not received any other information except for individual incidents. I think there was an IDV unit, that is to say, a reconnaissance sabotage unit, and disciplinary action was taken against them, about 20 of them. Out of that, 11 or 12 had been multiple offenders. I have the number of measures that were taken against that group of soldiers, but then I would have to look this up in my chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, do you believe that if you had been vigilant in ensuring that those soldiers responsible for forced trench-digging were punished in February and March of 1993, it would have prevented the extensive forced labour of Bosnian Muslims that took place at the hands of HVO soldiers in April and May of 1993? Do you think you could have prevented that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think so. It's not the way you put this question. I did my best to inform these armed peasants about their obligations in view of the Geneva Conventions and the treatment of detainees in respect of the Geneva Conventions, and from that point of view, every shift that was sent to the front line at Jajce, either I was there to see them off, particularly emphasising the question of a humane attitude, or I met them there before they came to Jajce and I personally addressed 100 or 200 persons specifically with regard to these matters. Also, I took preventive action, that is to say, I wanted to prevent such engagement of civilians or detainees, and I issued instructions during 1992, in December. There was a calendar in which I asked for all detainees to be treated in a humane way. There was a document we had here a few minutes ago, I don't know its number but it was dated August, that document shows that I took care of this, how the territory would be prepared for the soldiers to be staying there at the front line, but then the terrain would be prepared by the soldiers themselves, they would prepare shelter for themselves, and I emphasise that the other things were forbidden. Also, on the 5th of February, 1993, I issued such an order to the chief of staff and I prohibited such action. Whenever I received information of this nature, I took measures accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to the next document, General, which is the 23rd of January and the 24th of January, 1993, insertions into the diary of Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 675.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this is two diary entries, the first one being on 23 January, and General Stewart is discussing his visits to Gornji Vakuf. The second paragraph I'll start with. "Selmo was there but Colonel Siljeg didn't turn up until much later - having been picked up from beyond the minefield to the South of Gornji Vakuf. The battle is continuing in earnest. Parts of the BiH Army positions have fallen. The Croats are using a T55 tank to blast (the) hell out of the houses on the south edge of town. At the same time they are using artillery and multi-barreled rocket launchers in their attacks. Bistrica was struck twice whilst I was there. Within the camp perimeter, three mortar rounds landed today; and a round penetrated through --" I'm not sure what the next word is. "-- the sill of the Officers Mess window, struck a chair in which Selmo sat and 'pinged' around the room. All in all, Gornji Vakuf was not a particularly healthy place to be today. "When we finally got down to talking Siljeg was unbending. He demanded that the BiH Army centralise their weapons under his/our control. The BiH soldiers could stay there except that he wanted some for 'crimes'. I told him that was surrender in all but name. In addition I reminded him that the world would note who was attacking civilians; this was the first time I hinted at war crimes." If we could go to the bottom of the page for the entry on the 24th? Just that first paragraph: "Today I made my final effort to try and stop a holocaust in Gornji Vakuf. When I woke I felt that there was very little chance of success but all of us had to try. Before I left Vitez I tried to telephone Andrew Cumming or Richard Barrons to tell them what the situation was like. They were no available --" I'm sure it must be "not available." "-- and so I passed a message to the Watchkeeper stressing a number of points. To start with I suggested there was little hope of success in Gornji Vakuf. I complained that Colonel Siljeg seemed set on a battle and the 'capture' of the town. Ethnic cleansing and BM 21 strikes as well as tank attacks were taking place - all by the HVO.
